ComprehensionText:
The Comet's Promise
I am a comet, a snowball of dust,
far out where the cold planets roam.
I drift through the dark for a hundred long years,
but always I turn and come home.

Out past the giants with rings and with moons,
where sunlight is thin as a thread,
I sleep in the silence, as frozen as stone,
with nothing but stars overhead.

The Sun is a campfire I glimpse from afar,
a spark at the edge of the night.
It tugs at my coat with an invisible string
and reels me back into the light.

As I rush ever closer, my ice starts to melt,
and I steam like a pot on the boil.
A tail made of glitter streams out at my back,
a long, ghostly ribbon uncoiled.

My tail always points away from the Sun,
whichever direction I race,
as though a great wind from the Sun's glowing heart
were blowing the hair from my face.

On a planet of blue, little faces look up
and point at the streak in the sky.
I wish I could stay and say hello to them all,
but I only have time to fly by.

So I swing round the Sun and race out again,
my tail drifting after like smoke.
Remember my face, little planet of blue,
and the night that I passed and you woke.

The children who wave at me now will be old
when I come back this way once again,
so tell all their grandchildren, 'Look to the sky!'
for I promise that I'll see them then.
QuestionText: How long does the comet drift through the dark?
AnswerA: a hundred years
AnswerB: a single night
AnswerC: ten years
AnswerD: a thousand years

Subject: English
ComprehensionText:
Keep Cars on the Ground
Every few years, someone promises that flying cars are just around the corner. Videos show shiny machines zooming between skyscrapers. It looks thrilling, but I believe filling our skies with flying cars would be a big mistake.
Imagine it is the year 2075. Ten-year-old Priya steps outside her front door. Above her, hundreds of flying cars buzz like a swarm of angry bees. She cannot hear the birds or even her own thoughts. Her little brother covers his ears and refuses to walk to school. This is the noisy future we could be choosing.
Noise is only the first problem. A car with a flat tyre can pull over to the side of the road. A flying car with a broken engine has nowhere to go but down. Every driver would need far more training than drivers need today, and even skilled pilots make mistakes.
Flying cars would also use huge amounts of energy. Lifting a heavy vehicle into the air takes much more power than rolling it along a road. That means more batteries, more fuel and more harm to our planet.
Supporters say flying cars would end traffic jams. But the sky would soon fill up too, and a jam a hundred metres up is far more dangerous than one on the ground.
Instead of wasting billions on flying cars, let's build better trains, safer bike paths and quieter streets. The future should be calm, clean and safe, not buzzing over our heads.
QuestionText: Which reason does the writer give to show that flying cars would harm the planet?
AnswerA: Flying cars would be too noisy for birds.
AnswerB: Drivers would need much more training.
AnswerC: Lifting a vehicle takes more power than rolling it.
AnswerD: Engines could break down in the air.

Every few years, someone promises that flying cars are just around the corner. Videos show shiny machines zooming between skyscrapers. It looks thrilling, but I believe filling our skies with flying cars would be a big mistake.
Imagine it is the year 2075. Ten-year-old Priya steps outside her front door. Above her, hundreds of flying cars buzz like a swarm of angry bees. She cannot hear the birds or even her own thoughts. Her little brother covers his ears and refuses to walk to school. This is the noisy future we could be choosing.
Noise is only the first problem. A car with a flat tyre can pull over to the side of the road. A flying car with a broken engine has nowhere to go but down. Every driver would need far more training than drivers need today, and even skilled pilots make mistakes.
Flying cars would also use huge amounts of energy. Lifting a heavy vehicle into the air takes much more power than rolling it along a road. That means more batteries, more fuel and more harm to our planet.
Supporters say flying cars would end traffic jams. But the sky would soon fill up too, and a jam a hundred metres up is far more dangerous than one on the ground.
Instead of wasting billions on flying cars, let's build better trains, safer bike paths and quieter streets. The future should be calm, clean and safe, not buzzing over our heads.
QuestionText: The writer begins with videos of 'shiny machines zooming between skyscrapers' and ends by saying the future should not be 'buzzing over our heads'. What does this tell you about the writer's point of view?
AnswerA: The future that looks exciting in the videos is one the writer hopes we will not choose.
AnswerB: The writer thinks flying cars would be a problem only in cities with tall skyscrapers.
AnswerC: The writer enjoys the videos but is mostly worried about how much flying cars would cost.
AnswerD: The writer believes flying cars are coming soon, so we should get ready for them now.

ComprehensionText:
Nobody Held the Pen
The bees build rooms with six straight sides
and share each waxy wall,
a golden city, packed so tight
there's not a gap at all.
And nobody held the pen.

The snail's shell is a winding stair
that circles round and in;
it starts out wide, then turns and turns
and tightens to a pin.
And nobody held the pen.

A pebble dropped into the pond
sends rings that ripple out,
each circle wider than the last,
a whisper grown to a shout.
And nobody held the pen.

A snowflake lands upon my glove
with six arms, lacy-white,
each one a copy of the rest,
then melts before my sight.
And nobody held the pen.

A spider spins a silver wheel
of spokes and rings so fine,
each gap the same from hub to edge,
each thread a perfect line.
And nobody held the pen.

The sunflower packs its face with seeds
in spirals, row on row,
some curving left and some curving right,
like whirlpools as they grow.
And nobody held the pen.

The gum leaf has a map of roads
that branch from one thick vein,
like creeks seen from an aeroplane
across a dusty plain.
And nobody held the pen.

The wind combs ridges on the dunes
in long and wavy bands,
as even as the lines I trace
with fingers through the sand.
And nobody held the pen.

I use a ruler for my lines,
a compass for my rounds,
and still I rub out half of them
with grumbling, scratchy sounds.
So who was holding the pen?

AnswerD: a different animal building a home

Bread on the Goldfields
It was 1853, and the Ballarat goldfields were a sea of canvas tents and muddy holes. Every morning, Tom's father climbed down into their shaft with a pick and a bucket, hoping today would be the lucky day.
Tom's job was to rock the cradle. He tipped buckets of dirt and water into the wooden box and rocked it back and forth, so that any heavy gold would sink to the bottom. Most days, all he found was mud and stones. His arms ached, and his boots were always soaked.
Meanwhile, Tom's mother had an idea of her own. She built a clay oven behind their tent and began baking bread. The warm smell drifted across the diggings, and soon tired miners were lining up with coins in their hands. Some even paid with tiny flakes of gold.
One evening, Father climbed out of the shaft, empty-handed again. He sank onto a log with his head in his hands. Mum said nothing. She simply fetched the old tin box where she kept the bread money and tipped it onto the table. Coins and gold flakes spilled across the wood, glittering in the lamplight.
Father stared. Then he began to laugh.
'All this time I've been digging for gold,' he said, 'and you've been baking it.'
The next morning, Tom didn't rock the cradle. He chopped wood for the oven instead, whistling as he worked.
QuestionText: What was Tom's job at the start of the story?
AnswerA: rocking the cradle
AnswerB: baking the bread
AnswerC: digging the shaft
AnswerD: chopping the wood
